claims.text: The PGM nanoscale catalyst dynamically forms and regenerates surface metal-hydride intermediates during ethanol oxidation.
Surface metal-hydride intermediates facilitate proton-coupled electron-transfer steps in ethanol oxidation.
Dynamic hydride formation accounts for the catalyst's high ethanol-oxidation performance.
Disrupting the oxidation state that enables hydride formation will diminish catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
The initial catalyst has active sites in a balanced oxidation state that naturally promotes hydride formation.
Changing the applied electrochemical potential or using a chemical modifier can reduce the catalyst's ability to form surface hydrides.
A defined baseline potential favors hydride formation, whereas selected modified potentials disrupt hydride stability.
Transient surface metal hydrides induce local structural changes at catalyst active sites.
At the optimal potential, metal-hydride intermediates promote efficient transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons through proton-coupled electron-transfer pathways.
Alteration of the catalyst oxidation state interferes with hydride formation.
Interference with hydride formation reduces reaction efficiency, activity, selectivity, and durability.
At the baseline potential, spectroscopic hydride signals should correlate with high catalytic activity and selectivity.
Potential shifts that impede hydride formation should diminish hydride-associated spectroscopic signals and lower catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism operates only within a potential window that facilitates transient hydride formation.
At potentials that are too reducing or too oxidizing, performance may be governed by mechanisms unrelated to hydride formation.
Direct in-situ detection of transient hydrides is challenging, and other surface species may interfere with their spectroscopic measurement.
